tier_reason: Public code (src/mandel/{c_simd/main_simd.c,zig_simd/main_simd.zig,rust_simd/main_simd.rs,c_std/main.c,zig_std/main.zig}, Makefile, tools/runner.sh, tools/aggregate.py) with compilers and flags stated and raw hyperfine JSON in results/, but no CPU model anywhere, and it is a single-author, 0-star, one-commit suite written to showcase Zig, so first-party C, not A. Tier stays C; the claim is downgraded because the like-for-like rows show no language win.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mandelbrot 4000x4000, max_iter 1000, hyperfine mean of 20 runs (results/mandel_*.json): zig_simd_fast 1.922 s and zig_simd_safe 2.249 s vs c_simd_clang 3.261 s, c_simd_gcc 3.302 s, c_simd_zigcc 3.380 s and rust_simd 3.321 s, so the 8-lane Zig kernel is 1.70x to 1.76x faster than the 4-lane C kernels (ReleaseSafe 1.45x to 1.50x) (derived from page data); README ratios vs scalar gcc: 0.16x, 0.18x, 0.26x, 0.27x, 0.27x, 0.27x. Same-algorithm scalar rows are parity: zig_std_fast 12.374 s vs c_std_gcc 12.386 s (1.00x) and c_std_clang 12.631 s (1.02x). Other rows in the same suite (README ratios vs c_std_gcc): sieve zig_static_bitset_fast 0.63x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x but zig_std_fast 1.06x; btree zig_compact_fast 0.19x vs c_arena_gcc 0.21x; log_proc zig_std_fast 0.83x vs c_std_gcc 1.00x; atomics parity (0.97x to 1.00x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast (and ReleaseSafe) with no -target, so the host CPU is targeted (README: all binaries built for native); the SIMD kernel sets @setFloatMode(.strict). C SIMD: gcc 16.1.1 and clang 22.1.8 at -O3 -march=native -ffp-contract=off, zig cc -O3 -ffp-contract=off -march=native. C scalar: gcc/clang -O3 only (no -march=native), zig cc -O3 -ffp-contract=off. Rust 1.97.1: rust_simd rustc -C opt-level=3 -C target-cpu=native (no LTO); rust_std -C opt-level=3 -C lto=yes (Makefile). Measured with hyperfine --warmup 1 --min-runs 20 --output=null (tools/runner.sh); outputs are not checked against an expected checksum during timing.
corrections.caveats: Not like-for-like and not a language win. The Zig SIMD kernel (src/mandel/zig_simd/main_simd.zig) iterates an 8-lane @Vector(8, f64) block with u32 counters, which on AVX2 hardware compiles to two interleaved 4-wide chains (or one AVX-512 op if the unnamed CPU has it), while the C and Rust SIMD kernels (c_simd/main_simd.c, rust_simd/main_simd.rs) run a single 4-lane __m256d chain with 64-bit counters; the 1.7x gap is the extra ILP or width of the wider block, which the same C written with 8 lanes (two __m256d chains, AVX-512 intrinsics or GCC vector extensions) would also get. On the same algorithm with the same structure the scalar rows are parity (zig_std_fast 12.374 s vs c_std_gcc 12.386 s) even though the Zig scalar build targets the native CPU and the C scalar builds do not use -march=native. The sieve and btree wins come from different data layouts (a bitset instead of a byte array, 32-bit indices instead of 64-bit pointers), and the log_proc win compares Zig's std.fmt.bufPrint and parseUnsigned against glibc sprintf, strstr and atoi, so they are library and layout effects. Single commit (2026-08-20), 0 stars, CPU model not stated, no correctness check in the timed runs.
corrections.why_faster: Kernel shape, not the language: the Zig SIMD loop processes 8 f64 lanes per block (two independent AVX2 dependency chains or one AVX-512 vector) against one 4-lane AVX2 chain in the C and Rust intrinsics versions, so it hides FP latency better. With equal structure (scalar rows) Zig and C are at parity. The README's explanation (clearer intent to LLVM, better register renaming) is not supported by any equal-width comparison.

notes: Numbers match the README and the raw hyperfine JSON (zig_simd_fast 1.922 s, c_simd_gcc 3.302 s, c_std_gcc 12.386 s). Shortcomings to record: unequal SIMD kernels (8-lane Zig vs 4-lane C/Rust), scalar like-for-like rows at parity, sieve/btree/log_proc wins come from data layout or library differences, CPU model not stated, single-commit 0-star suite, timed runs not checked for correct output; same_algorithm corrected to false, same_opt_level true for the SIMD rows (all three at native with strict FP), rust_simd has no LTO.

tier_reason: The README table and raw wrk files (results/E5-1650v2-Ubuntu-14.04LTS/netty_04.txt 422,580 req/s, nginx_echo_01.txt 381,368, crow_*.txt) carry the numbers and the code is public, but compiler versions and the JVM are unstated, the suite is a 53-star single-author repo rather than a well-known one, the nginx baseline is handicapped by its config (4 workers) and the measured artifact is the legacy Netty 3 jar, not the current netty/netty code, so C rather than B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 422,580 req/s (99th percentile 4.08 ms) vs nginx with the echo module 381,368 (1.11x, derived from page data) and Crow 256,552 (1.65x, derived from page data); slower than the C servers Kore 572,782 (0.74x), libmicrohttpd 533,626 (0.79x) and Onion 483,824 (0.87x) in the same table (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Netty side: benchmarks/netty/build.gradle pulls org.jboss.netty:netty:latest.integration (the legacy Netty 3 artifact under the old JBoss groupId, before Netty moved to io.netty) plus Guice and Guava 'latest.integration', run with 'gradle run'; JVM version and flags not stated. Crow: c++ -O3 -std=c++11 with boost_system and pthread, multithreaded() (benchmarks/crow/run.sh, helloworld.cpp); compiler version not stated (Ubuntu 14.04 toolchain implied). nginx: the OpenResty nginx binary at /usr/local/openresty/nginx/sbin/nginx with the echo module, worker_processes 4 (benchmarks/nginx/run_echo.sh, conf/echo.conf); version and build flags not stated.
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1650 v2 @ 3.50 GHz (6 cores, 12 threads; results/E5-1650v2-Ubuntu-14.04LTS and commit 'All recent results were on E5-1650v2'), 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16; wrk on the same machine with 12 threads (thread count from common/threads.sh, shown in the raw wrk output) and 100 connections, a 10 s warm-up then four 20 s runs (time.sh).
corrections.workload: Trivial dynamic 'Hello World' text/plain response over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with wrk, 12 threads and 100 connections on the same host, framework overhead only; the nginx echo row answers 'Hello World!' as text/html with the Date and Server headers cleared, so bytes per response differ.
corrections.caveats: Measured in December 2015 (last results commit 2015-12-22) with the legacy Netty 3 artifact org.jboss.netty:netty resolved through 'latest.integration', so the numbers describe neither Netty 4.x nor the current netty/netty code. The nginx baseline is handicapped: conf/echo.conf sets worker_processes 4 on a 6-core/12-thread Xeon while Netty 3's NioServerSocketChannelFactory uses a cached thread pool with its default worker count, and nginx is the OpenResty build with the echo module, not a tuned stock nginx; its 24.24 ms p99 against Netty's 4.08 ms points to worker saturation. Load generator (wrk, 12 threads) shares the host. JVM, Netty, Crow, OpenResty and compiler versions are not stated; the README table matches single runs (netty_04, nginx_echo_01). Crow is the 2015 ipkn/crow submodule, built -O3 and multithreaded, which is the fairer comparison. Netty loses to all three C servers (Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion), so it is not faster than C servers in general. Single-author suite with 53 stars, not a well-known third-party benchmark.

notes: Numbers match the README and raw wrk files. Shortcomings to record: legacy Netty 3 jar (org.jboss.netty, latest.integration) measured, not current Netty; 2015 data; nginx limited to worker_processes 4 on a 12-thread CPU (crippled baseline config) and run as OpenResty with the echo module; load generator on the same host; versions and compiler flags unstated; Netty slower than Kore, libmicrohttpd and Onion. Only the Crow row (1.65x, -O3, multithreaded) is a fair C++ comparison.

corrections.caveats: The baseline-h2c rows in quarkus-jvm.json (and its json-h2c and unary-grpc rows) were last written no later than the 2026-07-24 migration commit 5698fa8 and cannot come from the current entry: its Dockerfile has passed -Dvertx.disableH2c=true since at least 2026-03-28, application.properties opens no port 8082 (the h2c prior-knowledge port), and meta.json no longer subscribes to baseline-h2c, json-h2c or grpc; every h2c row also reports p99 equal to the mean, unlike nginx's h2c rows measured on 2026-08-20, so the 2.52x h2c ratio is a cross-run comparison against stale data. The remaining wins are on pipelining (reference-only in the HttpArena README) and h2 over TLS, where nginx's HTTP/2 path trails h2o by 4.7x on the same profile; on the scored HTTP/1.1 baseline, limited-conn, json-tls and static profiles Quarkus is 0.21x to 0.55x of nginx. The entry's meta.json and README say JDK 21 but the Dockerfile runs Temurin 25. nginx is a custom C handler module, not a stock config; every entry is a minimal hand-written handler, so this measures server-engine overhead, not static-file serving. Results are 5 s runs on one machine, rerun per framework by the maintainers.
corrections.why_faster: Netty event loops under Vert.x with JVM tuning; the suite gives no mechanism. The h2 win reflects nginx's comparatively slow HTTP/2 implementation (h2o is 4.7x nginx on baseline-h2-256), and the pipelined win comes from a reference-only 16x pipelining profile; not a language or JIT effect that the suite isolates.
